frameworks.name: Solomon Framework
frameworks.definition: A weekly self-advisory practice in which the practitioner simulates conversation with their 85-year-old future self (named Solomon) to obtain advice that satisfies all three criteria for good counsel: competence, context, and alignment.

frameworks.name: Three Criteria for Good Advice
frameworks.definition: Any advice source must simultaneously satisfy competence (knowing the domain), context (knowing your specific situation), and alignment (having incentives that match yours); failure on any one criterion compromises the quality of guidance received.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that any source of advice must satisfy three simultaneous requirements to be trusted: competence (expertise in the domain), context (detailed knowledge of your specific situation), and alignment (incentives that are genuinely pointed toward your benefit). A source that satisfies competence and context but lacks alignment is especially dangerous because it can cause targeted harm.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: A misaligned advisor who is both competent and context-rich knows exactly what would hurt you and has no incentive to avoid it, making the advice actively harmful rather than merely useless.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that conventional therapy models frequently fail all three advice criteria simultaneously: the therapist may be less competent than the client in the client's specific domain, lacks deep ongoing context (requiring 90 minutes of background per session), and is financially incentivized to extend the relationship rather than resolve it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applied to high-competence individuals seeking domain-specific decision support, not mental health treatment
claims.mechanism: Therapist income depends on repeat sessions, creating structural misalignment between client's goal (resolution) and provider's goal (continuation).
bounded_by: Does not apply to clinical mental health treatment contexts where domain expertise clearly exceeds client's

claims.text: The Solomon Paradox, a documented psychological effect, demonstrates that people give better advice about their own problems when those problems are presented to them as belonging to a third party. Research feeding subjects back their own life statistics as a whiteout character shows subjects recommend superior decisions compared to those they actually make for themselves.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Psychological distance from a problem reduces ego-protective distortion, enabling more objective analysis of the same information.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the 85-year-old future self (his Solomon) uniquely satisfies all three criteria for good advice simultaneously: competence (knows the full arc of outcomes), context (knows every detail of the situation), and alignment (has no competing incentives since it is oneself).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Future-self projection combines the Solomon Paradox's psychological distance with perfect contextual knowledge and zero incentive misalignment, eliminating all three failure modes of external advice.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that most individuals already know what they should do in a given situation; the primary obstacle is not ignorance but willingness to act on that knowledge without external validation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that humans can easily enroll friends, therapists, and even themselves in a self-serving story that diverges from the actual truth of a situation, and that the Solomon practice bypasses this self-enrollment because one part of the practitioner genuinely knows the real truth regardless of the constructed narrative.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The future-self persona cannot be misled by the present self's rationalizations because it shares the same underlying knowledge base; the psychological distance forces honest appraisal that social relationships allow the practitioner to avoid.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for high achievers, external validation loses its motivational power once early success is established; the only remaining bar to clear is one's own internal standard, specifically the gap between how hard one tried versus how hard effort only appears to outside observers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to individuals who have achieved sufficient external success that social approval no longer functions as a primary motivator
claims.mechanism: External observers cannot distinguish between maximum effort and effort that appears maximum; only the actor holds ground truth on the gap, so internal standards become the sole meaningful accountability mechanism.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that his chosen personal success criterion is leaving with nothing left in reserve at death, framed as closing the Delta between how hard he actually tried versus how hard his efforts could look from outside. He does not expect to be remembered by others and does not use posterity as a motivation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi, drawing on Don Miguel Ruiz's concept of ruthless self-love, argues that genuine self-accountability requires the simultaneous capacity to affirm that one gave everything (compassion) and to identify where one could have tried harder (confrontation), without allowing either to suppress the other.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that removing the external judgment layer (what other people think) by reasoning through the Solomon persona converts abstract social fears into named specific individuals, which immediately deflates their decision-making power. Once a fear is attributed to a specific named person, the practitioner can directly evaluate whether that person's opinion warrants the behavioral constraint.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Abstract social fear (what will people think) functions as an inflated threat because it is amorphous; naming the specific individuals (e.g., Tom, John) reduces the fear to a concrete, evaluable question about one actual person's opinion, which typically fails the evaluation.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the thing one wants to do and the thing that everyone else thinks one should do are usually different, and that the crowd's consensus is probably not the right course of action for the individual.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi describes a Solomon-based gratitude practice in which he imagines his 85-year-old future self reborn into the present moment and re-experiencing current circumstances with aged perspective, causing ordinary present-day situations (a young spouse, a pain-free body, a city's skyline) to register as remarkable rather than routine.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Offered as an alternative for individuals who struggle with conventional gratitude journaling
claims.mechanism: Perspective adoption from an aged future state makes familiar stimuli novel by temporarily restoring the contrast that hedonic adaptation has erased.

examples.text: Alex Hormozi describes a multi-year project he had built significant anticipation around. A vendor had made a promise that others had successfully relied upon in identical circumstances, so trusting the vendor appeared reasonable. The vendor failed to deliver, costing Hormozi approximately $15 million of real money. He worked through the disappointment using a Solomon session. His future self, knowing the full investment of time and effort, said: I am the product that you were building, not the thing. And I know what you put into that. And I am satisfied. And that is enough. Hormozi reports this was sufficient to resolve the emotional weight of the loss.

Alex Hormozi describes a period when he was weighing whether to sell his company. He identified hesitation but could not pinpoint its source. Using the Solomon framework, he traced the hesitation to concern about what two specific individuals (referred to by first names John and Tom) would think of the decision. He then asked whether he wanted those two specific people's opinions to be the reason he did not act. He concluded it was not rational to allow that and proceeded accordingly.

Alex Hormozi describes a Solomon session that resolved in seven minutes. Rather than requiring extended exploration, he reached a clear answer quickly and the session ended. He notes that session length varies widely, with some sessions being brief and some requiring extended exploration, driven by when a genuine resolution is reached rather than a fixed time allocation.

practices.text: Block the first hour of every Monday on your calendar, labeled Solomon. Use it to conduct a written dialogue simulating conversation with your 85-year-old future self. Write as yourself, then respond as your future self, iterating until you reach a genuine resolution rather than a rationalized one.

When naming a social fear (what will people think), force yourself to name the actual individuals whose opinion you are deferring to, then evaluate whether each specific person's opinion genuinely warrants the behavioral constraint you are imposing on yourself.

As a variation on conventional gratitude journaling, imagine yourself as your 85-year-old future self who has been reborn into your present-day life. Walk through ordinary morning experiences (waking next to your partner, looking out the window, noticing physical pain is absent) from that aged perspective to restore appreciation that hedonic adaptation has eroded.

Continue a Solomon session until you reach a resolution that you cannot talk yourself out of, not just a comfortable stopping point. If a part of you suspects you are still enrolled in your own story, keep pushing.
